description:
We are a team of Informatics students passionate about building innovative, impactful solutions using technology and NASA’s open data. Our interests include Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Web Development, Data Science, and UI/UX Design.

We aim to develop a solution that combines technical innovation, scientific research, and real-world impact for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We value collaboration, creativity, curiosity, and a willingness to learn
summary: JalaWatch is an interactive web dashboard that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar to monitor floating net fish cages in Jatiluhur Reservoir, West Java, Indonesia. Overcrowded cages have been linked to water-quality problems and mass fish deaths, and frequent cloud cover makes the reservoir hard to monitor with optical satellites. Answering the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, JalaWatch turns NISAR radar data into an interactive map of a changing water surface: cage frames appear as bright targets on dark, calm water, and L-band radar sees through clouds. From a 6 November 2026 NISAR Level-2 GCOV scene, our pipeline derives the reservoir outline from the radar itself, detects 739 bright cage blocks, and estimates about 34,248 cages (assuming 100 m² per cage). The dashboard shows results by zone, with totals, density, and CSV, GeoJSON, PNG, and GeoTIFF downloads. This matters because it can help the fisheries office, the reservoir manager, researchers, and communities target inspections before overcrowding worsens. Only one date is processed so far; NISAR’s 12-day repeat makes tracking cage change over time the next step.
details:
1. Project Overview

JalaWatch is a public web application that maps and counts floating net fish cages (keramba jaring apung) on Jatiluhur Reservoir in Purwakarta, West Java, Indonesia, using NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar. Built for the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, it is an interactive application that uses NISAR data to begin tracking and visualizing surface change on a working reservoir. It has two parts: an offline Python pipeline that turns NISAR products into open data files, and a static website that presents those files as an interactive dashboard.

2. Problem Statement

Floating net cages are an important source of income around Jatiluhur, but overcrowded cages have been linked to water-quality problems and mass fish deaths. Managers need to know how many cages there are and where they are concentrated, yet field counts are slow and optical satellite images are often blocked by the clouds and haze common over tropical Indonesia. There is no cheap, repeatable, cloud-independent way for the fisheries office, the reservoir manager (PJT II), researchers, and communities to see cage numbers and density.

3. Proposed Solution

JalaWatch uses NISAR L-band radar, which sees through clouds. In radar images, calm water is dark, while metal and plastic cage frames produce bright returns. JalaWatch detects these bright targets inside the reservoir, estimates the number of cages, groups them by zone, and shows the results on a map with totals, density, and status colors (Safe, Watch, or Over limit). All results can be downloaded as CSV, GeoJSON, PNG, and GeoTIFF.

4. How It Works

Data: a NISAR Level-2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance (GCOV) granule acquired on 6 November 2026 (NISAR_L2_PR_GCOV_035_018_D_092_4005_DHDH_A_20261106T111143_20261106T111222_P05036_N_F_J_001.h5; L-band HH and HV; 10 m grid in UTM zone 48S, EPSG:32748), downloaded from the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) through NASA Earthdata.

Reservoir mask: the HH layer is converted to decibels and median filtered; water is HH below −13 dB; after hole filling, the largest connected water body is kept, the river channel is removed, and the shoreline is trimmed, giving about 53 km² of reservoir. The outline is split into five illustrative zones (Zone 1 West to Zone 5 East).

Cage detection: inside the mask, pixels with HH above −8 dB are bright targets. Eight-connected bright pixels form candidate cage blocks, and blocks smaller than 4 pixels are dropped, leaving 739 blocks. Each block’s area is divided by an assumed 100 m² per cage, and counts are summed per zone and smoothed into a density grid.

Result for 6 November 2026: about 34,248 estimated cages (Zone 1 West 8,849; Zone 2 6,672; Zone 3 7,219; Zone 4 6,863; Zone 5 East 4,645). A bright, gridded area on the west arm is excluded pending verification.

Website: the outputs are static JSON, GeoJSON, CSV, PNG, and GeoTIFF files loaded by a Vite website with a Leaflet map, Chart.js charts, and GSAP scroll animation, deployed on Vercel. Users can select zones, see totals and density, view zones over the illustrative limit, and download the data.

5. Benefits and Impact

JalaWatch gives a cheap, repeatable, cloud-independent view of cage numbers and density. It can help the fisheries office and the reservoir manager target inspections toward the most crowded areas before pollution and fish kills worsen, gives researchers open, downloadable data, and makes the situation visible to local communities. Because NISAR revisits every 12 days, the same pipeline can show where cages are added or removed over time. The method could be extended to the other Citarum cascade reservoirs, Cirata and Saguling.

6. Technology and Tools Used

Data: NASA-ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV from ASF / NASA Earthdata. Backend: Python with h5py, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, Shapely, pyproj, and Pillow (Matplotlib for quick-look images); unit tests with Python unittest. Frontend: Vite, Leaflet, Chart.js, and GSAP, with locally bundled fonts (Unbounded, Plus Jakarta Sans, IBM Plex Mono). Testing: Playwright browser checks. Hosting and code: Vercel and GitHub. AI assistance: OpenAI Codex CLI and Grok Bot (see Use of Super Intelligence).

7. Innovation and Creativity

JalaWatch derives the reservoir outline from the NISAR radar itself instead of relying on outside maps, then counts cages with a transparent, reproducible thresholding method whose parameters are published with the results. It applies brand-new NISAR L-band data to a local aquaculture problem that optical satellites struggle with because of clouds. The sonar-themed interface turns radar outputs into a story that non-specialists can follow, and the whole system runs as a static site with no server or database, which makes it cheap to host and easy to reproduce.

8. Design Considerations

Honesty about uncertainty: the site labels the result as an automated estimate that needs field validation, states that zones and capacity limits are illustrative rather than official PJT II values, and explains that each map dot is a candidate cage block, not a single cage. Reproducibility: the exact command and parameters are in the README and in summary.json. Accessibility and performance: the site is responsive, respects “prefers-reduced-motion”, uses local map geometry with no online tiles, and bundles its fonts. Limitations we report openly: only one date is processed so far, the 100 m² per cage factor is an assumption, and results have not been checked against field surveys; wind, boats, shoreline double bounce, and other structures can also look bright in radar.
